items.title: 52035_Eddie Durham oral history interview
items.q: And I used to play (unintelligible) with Teddy Wilson -- In the rhythm section and Teddy Wilson playing piano.

ctx.x: Well, I was kind of a rolling stone, you know? Like, after you play with a band so long, I say, man, this band is at a standstill, I want to find something bigger and more exciting. I'd heard Duke Ellington, you know, and I wanted to leave because I said, the band has got all you need. Say, all right, give me some good arrangements if you got to leave me. I say, well, I'll leave you Pat. And that's when Buster was there, we all got together with things like Morton Swing and a few of those things, and Lafayette,…
And then I went to New York. I think Willie Pratt sent for me, and that's when he had the band -- and Billy Carter was in his band. Teddy Wilson and Cozy Coles and Battles.

items.title: 66600_Teddy Wilson oral history interview
items.q: Interviewer mentions: '...very few people know of Benny Moten or Eddie Durham'

ctx.x: I notice that in jazz, like for instance, you commented to Steven that Coltrane is his era -- you hear these bands like in North State Texas and so forth, all of them playing very well, doing the compositions of Thayer Jones, and all the people, with the Maynard Ferguson sound and the like -- but you never hear anybody play anything like Ben Moten or Fletcher Henderson, like Jay McShann, by anybody, or even the lesser known bands further back. And I find that you see, when the rock era came in, all this sort of…

And in the classical world, they've never said you're moving forward because the other is inferior. You add to it, but you keep it all together and the great masters of Europe that go all the way back to Michael Praetorius, even back to the Gregorian period, are still preserved to this day, but yet, very few people know of Benny Moten or Eddie Durham, and any of these people --
That should be taught at Berklee
